subject: mathematics
title: 6.1 Introduction to Trigonometry — Ratios & Complementary Angles
subtitle: History (Hipparchus & Aryabhata Jya), 6 trigonometric ratios, and visual complementary-angle proof (pp. 239–241)
curiosity_hook: Why do all right-angled triangles with the same acute angle θ share the exact same sine, cosine, and tangent ratios no matter how large or small the triangle is?
source_verified_by: AGY Pass 2 Full-Chapter Build (pending human maths teacher sign-off)
learning_objectives: Recall and compute all six trigonometric ratios (sin, cos, tan, cosec, sec, cot) of an acute angle 0° < θ < 90° in right triangle OMP.
Derive complementary angle relationships such as sin(90° − θ) = cos θ using the unit-semicircle rectangle proof (pp. 240–241).
Recall exact ratio values for standard angles 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90°.

concept_outline.heading: Origins of Trigonometry & Similarity Invariance (pp. 239–240)
concept_outline.summary: Hipparchus of Rhodes (~200 BCE) built early chord tables, Indian astronomers including Aryabhata refined half-chords ('Jya' → Latin 'sinus' → sine), and Bartholomaeus Pitiscus coined 'Trigonometry'. Because all right triangles with acute angle θ are similar, ratios depend ONLY on θ.

concept_outline.heading: The Six Fundamental Ratios (p. 240)
concept_outline.summary: From sin θ = Opp/Hyp and cos θ = Adj/Hyp come tan θ = sin θ / cos θ, cot θ = cos θ / sin θ, cosec θ = 1 / sin θ, and sec θ = 1 / cos θ.

concept_outline.heading: Complementary Angle Visual Proof (pp. 240–241)
concept_outline.summary: In rectangle OPQR inscribed in a unit semicircle (OQ = 1), OP = cos θ = RQ = sin(90° − θ) and PQ = sin θ = OR = cos(90° − θ). Likewise tan(90° − θ) = cot θ and sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ.

key_terms.definition: Scale-invariant ratio of two sides of a right-angled triangle determined strictly by acute angle θ.
Two acute angles summing to 90° (θ and 90° − θ), where sin(90° − θ) = cos θ.
Ancient Indian half-chord term ('Jya') that evolved through Arabic 'jiba' and Latin 'sinus' into modern 'sine'.

controls.label: Acute Angle θ Slider & Presets
controls.description: Vary θ from 5° to 85° and inspect all 6 ratios alongside complementary angle (90° − θ).
controls.keyboard_equivalent: Arrow Left/Right on slider or Enter on 30°/45°/60° presets.

expected_observations: Setting θ = 30° gives sin(30°) = 0.5000 = cos(60°), verifying sin(θ) = cos(90° − θ).
At θ = 45°, Opposite equals Adjacent, so sin(45°) = cos(45°) ≈ 0.7071 and tan(45°) = 1.
limitations: Right-triangle visualizer covers acute angles 5°–85°; exact boundary values at 0° and 90° are summarized in the standard table.

storyboard.title: Test θ = 30° and θ = 60°
storyboard.learner_action: Click θ = 30° then θ = 60° and compare sin and cos readouts.

storyboard.title: Sweep θ Continuously
storyboard.learner_action: Drag θ from 20° to 70° and observe tan θ = sin θ / cos θ.
storyboard.expected_response: Reciprocal pairs (sin·cosec = 1, cos·sec = 1, tan·cot = 1) hold at every angle.

accessible_equivalent.summary: Complete standard ratio table (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°), reciprocal definitions, and complementary-angle equations.

steps.heading: Primary Ratios
steps.description: sin θ = Opp/Hyp, cos θ = Adj/Hyp, tan θ = Opp/Adj = sin θ / cos θ.
steps.key_takeaway: All similar right triangles give identical ratios for the same θ.

steps.heading: Reciprocal Ratios
steps.description: cosec θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ.
steps.key_takeaway: Every reciprocal product equals 1 for 0° < θ < 90°.

steps.heading: Complementary Pairs
steps.description: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ; tan(90° − θ) = cot θ; sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ.
steps.key_takeaway: Complementary angles swap sine↔cosine, tangent↔cotangent, secant↔cosecant.

question_bank.prompt: Who is regarded as 'The Father of Trigonometry' in Class 10 Mathematics (p. 239) for constructing chord tables?
question_bank.hint: Greek astronomer of Rhodes around 200 BCE.

options.label: Hipparchus of Rhodes
options.feedback: Correct! Hipparchus (~200 BCE) built chord tables forming the foundation of trigonometry.

options.label: Pappus of Alexandria
options.feedback: Pappus is featured in Chapter 7 (Mensuration), p. 269.

options.label: Joseph Fourier
options.feedback: Fourier is quoted on p. 239, not called the Father of Trigonometry.

options.label: Bartholomaeus Pitiscus
options.feedback: Pitiscus coined the word 'Trigonometry' in the 17th century.

question_bank.worked_explanation: Textbook p. 239 credits Hipparchus of Rhodes (~200 BCE) as the Father of Trigonometry.

question_bank.prompt: Using complementary angle identities (p. 240), what is the exact value of sin(37°) / cos(53°)?

options.feedback: Neither numerator nor denominator is zero.
Correct! Since 53° = 90° − 37°, cos(53°) = sin(37°), so the ratio equals 1.
They are equal quantities divided by each other.

question_bank.prompt: Why do trigonometric ratios of an acute angle θ NOT change if you double all three side lengths of the right triangle?
question_bank.hint: Think about similar triangles (Note on p. 240).

options.label: Because the scale factor cancels out in every ratio of two sides of similar right triangles
options.feedback: Correct! (2·Opp)/(2·Hyp) = Opp/Hyp — all right triangles with angle θ are similar.

options.label: Because θ also doubles
options.feedback: Scaling all sides proportionally keeps all interior angles unchanged.

options.label: Because sine only uses the hypotenuse
options.feedback: Sine is the ratio of Opposite to Hypotenuse.

options.label: Only when θ = 45°
options.feedback: Similarity invariance holds for every acute angle 0° < θ < 90°.

question_bank.worked_explanation: All right triangles sharing acute angle θ are AA-similar, so corresponding side ratios stay invariant.

worked_feedback: Memorize sin θ for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° as √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2 and reverse the row for cos θ.

flashcards.front: Exact values of sin 30°, sin 45°, sin 60°

flashcards.back: sin(90°−θ) = cos θ; tan(90°−θ) = cot θ; sec(90°−θ) = cosec θ.
